title: 'Flock Flocked up'

reading.body:
This is a false-positive match in an automated licence plate reader, compounded by the human response that followed it. The failure occurred at the point where an alert from the camera system was treated as a confirmed fact about a vehicle and its occupants. The system reported a stolen plate, and the officers acted on that report before verifying it against the vehicle in front of them. The mismatch was visible in the alert itself: the camera image showed a Chevy Malibu while the plate was on a red Dodge Ram pickup.

Catching this would not have required new technology. It would have required an officer to compare the vehicle description attached to the alert with the vehicle being stopped, a check that the reporting suggests did not happen before weapons were drawn and the dog was deployed. The department's own K-9 policy sets conditions for deployment, including the severity of the crime, the immediacy of any threat, and whether a suspect is resisting or evading. Whether those conditions were met is a question the internal investigation answered in the negative for wrongdoing, and the facts given do not resolve it either way.

What is not established is intent, and the reports do not show whether the misread was a known limitation of the system, whether officers were trained to verify alerts, or what the department concluded about the camera's role. An internal finding of no wrongdoing is not a finding that the alert was accurate, and dropped charges are not a ruling on the stop.

reports.title: Body cam of TPD officers releasing K-9 on man during traffic stop
Man speaks out after police release K-9 on him during traffic stop: 'Traumatized'
TPD investigation finds no wrongdoing in use of K-9 on man during traffic stop
Charges dropped against man Toledo Police released K-9 on during traffic stop, lawyer says

summary:
Toledo Police released body camera video showing officers drawing guns and using a K-9 on a driver during a traffic stop. The stop began after a FLOCK camera alert about a stolen plate, but the report says the alert was wrong. The camera image matched a Chevy Malibu while the plate was actually on a red Dodge Ram pickup. The driver, Brandon Upchurch, got out with his hands up, was ordered to the ground, and was then arrested and charged with resisting arrest and obstruction. He received medical attention at the scene.

Officers later realized the plate information was a misread and was not stolen. Police said they thought Upchurch might flee and did not know if he or a passenger had weapons. The article notes that TPD's K-9 policy requires handlers to weigh the crime's severity, any immediate threat, and whether a suspect is resisting or trying to evade arrest before deploying the dog. The article does not say what happens next.
